slides.title: Ronan learns to align movement with sound
body: **Rhythmic entrainment** is the adjustment of a repeating movement to an external rhythm. Ronan, a California sea lion, learned to move her head up and down while hearing regularly spaced sounds. The lowest point of each movement supplied a repeatable timing marker.

Cook and colleagues trained this behavior at 80 and 120 beats per minute, then tested other rates and musical recordings. A movement that stays aligned across unfamiliar rates requires flexible timing rather than the repetition of one memorized motor speed.

Ronan lived at the University of California, Santa Cruz. The experimental task underlying her public reputation as a dancing sea lion combined a controlled sound sequence, concealed trainers, video measurements, and food reinforcement for appropriately timed behavior.

slides.title: Matching tempo differs from matching the beat
body: **Tempo** is the repetition rate of the sound sequence, expressed in beats per minute. Matching tempo means producing the same average number of movements per unit time. Two repeating events can share a tempo while occurring at different points within each cycle.

**Phase** describes the position of a movement relative to the sound cycle. Synchronization requires a stable timing relationship, ideally with the selected movement landmark near sound onset. The 2013 study measured both the movement rate and its alignment with individual beats.

At different unfamiliar tempos, Ronan maintained organized phase relationships even when her head reached its lowest point before or after the sound. These offsets distinguish successful coordination with the repeating stimulus from exact coincidence at the beat itself.

slides.title: A folded cortex overlies a large cerebellum
body: **Neuroanatomy** is the organization of the nervous system and its structures. **Cerebral cortex** is the outer sheet of the cerebrum. Sawyer and colleagues examined a juvenile California sea-lion brain whose cortical surface contained numerous folds. **Gyri** are the raised folds; **sulci** are the grooves separating them. The two hemispheres had similar but nonidentical groove patterns.

The fixed specimen was 10.2 cm long and 10.1 cm wide near its posterior end, compared with 6.0 cm across the anterior portion. These are dimensions of the preserved juvenile specimen, rather than measurements of Ronan or a standard adult brain.

A large **cerebellum**, a brain structure involved in movement coordination, lay beneath the posterior cerebral region. The study localized sensory cortex using tissue stains and anatomical landmarks. Folding alone did not locate functional regions; microscopic organization supplied the boundaries of the somatosensory area.

slides.title: Whisker follicles connect touch to the trigeminal nerve
body: **Vibrissae** are specialized whiskers whose follicles receive sensory innervation. The examined sea lions had 38 whiskers arranged in six rows on each cheek pad. Their facial array provides many separate points at which contact or water movement can deform a whisker.

A stained follicle contained a blood-filled cavernous sinus and a deep vibrissal nerve entering its base. This structure differs from an ordinary coat-hair follicle. Whisker deformation is therefore delivered to an innervated sensory organ embedded in the skin rather than detected by the hair shaft itself.

The **trigeminal nerve** carries facial somatosensory signals, meaning information about touch and related bodily sensation. Its thick sensory root lay beside a separate, smaller motor root. **Axons** are nerve-cell fibers that conduct signals; **myelin** is their insulating sheath. Microscopy identified thinly and thickly myelinated axons in the pathway carrying facial information into the brainstem.

slides.title: Brainstem modules organize facial sensory input
body: The **principal sensory trigeminal nucleus** is a brainstem relay for facial somatosensory information. In sea-lion tissue, this nucleus contained clusters separated by relatively cell-sparse partitions. Related modules also occurred in the spinal trigeminal nuclei, which extend the facial representation through the brainstem.

**Nissl staining** reveals neuronal cell bodies. **Cytochrome oxidase staining** marks metabolic organization, while vesicular glutamate transporter 1 staining identified dense afferent terminal regions. **Glutamate** is a neurotransmitter, a chemical signal released at synapses. This transporter packages it in presynaptic vesicles. The three preparations converged on a modular architecture instead of a uniform mass of tissue.

The arrangement resembled the facial whisker array, especially the six-row organization in the interpolaris subdivision. Individual sections did not yield an exact whisker-to-module assignment. The anatomical finding is a partitioned facial sensory representation, with dense incoming terminals concentrated within its modules.

slides.title: The thalamus separates face and body representations
body: The **thalamus** contains relays between ascending sensory pathways and cerebral cortex. The sea-lion **ventral posterior nucleus** was distinguished from surrounding tissue by large neuronal cell bodies and dense staining for cytochrome oxidase and vesicular glutamate transporter 2.

Its **ventroposterior medial subdivision**, or VPM, occupied a large part of the nucleus and corresponds to facial representation in the mammalian somatosensory pathway. The neighboring **ventroposterior lateral subdivision**, or VPL, corresponds to bodily representation. Their boundaries changed across successive sections rather than forming identical shapes at every depth.

Lightly stained partitions divided the nucleus internally. The sea-lion preparation established these subdivisions anatomically, without a physiological point-by-point body map. Facial sensation thus has an extensive thalamic territory between its brainstem representation and the cortical sensory region.

slides.title: Sensory cortical layer 4 receives dense input
body: **Primary somatosensory cortex**, or S1, is a cerebral region receiving bodily sensory information. Sawyer and colleagues localized a presumptive S1 region just anterior to the major vertical fissure using its microscopic organization and position within the folded sea-lion cortex.

**Cortical layers** are bands that differ in neuronal populations and connections. In this region, layer 4 contained densely packed cells and stained strongly for cytochrome oxidase and vesicular glutamate transporter 2. Layer 5 was relatively cell-sparse, whereas layer 6 was thick and cell-dense.

The VGLUT2-rich layer identifies a concentration of glutamatergic input terminals associated with primary sensory cortex. Tissue organization therefore connected a macroscopically folded surface with a specific sensory territory. Reconstructing successive stained sections placed that territory relative to the coronal and suprasylvian sulci.

slides.title: Brain rhythms change with arousal state
body: **Electroencephalography**, or EEG, records voltage fluctuations through electrodes near the head. Williams and colleagues adapted the electrode arrangement to California sea lions and identified patterns in neurologically normal animals alongside recordings from animals with neurological disease.

Wakeful recordings included low-amplitude **beta activity**, faster than 13 Hz, interspersed with **alpha activity** at 8–13 Hz. Slow-wave sleep contained high-amplitude **delta activity**, slower than 4 Hz, and sleep spindles around 12–14 Hz. The same nervous system can therefore produce different temporal activity patterns across states.

These EEG rhythms are electrical activity patterns, whereas Ronan’s entrainment is a measured relationship between movement and an external sound sequence. The distinction separates physiological frequency from behavioral beat keeping. Sedation and arousal were tracked because they altered the EEG state being interpreted.

slides.title: Touch exploration changes with the sensory task
body: **Active sensing** means moving a sensory organ to acquire information relevant to a task. Lo, a California sea lion, used different head and whisker movements when discriminating texture, size, or visual brightness. Blindfolds restricted the texture and size tasks to tactile exploration.

For texture, Lo swept laterally across the surfaces. For size, she moved toward the object edges and made larger whisker movements. Average whisker excursions were about 34° for texture and 47° for size, compared with 24° during visual brightness discrimination.

The target remained the intermediate stimulus among two distractors. A visual control reduced the need to explore by touch, and head and whisker movements declined. Task-specific movement therefore changed how the sensory surface was sampled, linking perceptual demands to the motor strategy used to solve them.

slides.title: A learned command initiates sensory-guided choice
body: A **learned command** is a cue associated with a trained action or task. In Lo’s discrimination experiment, the trainer used “find it” to initiate exploration after the stimuli had been placed underwater. The command started a task whose solution still depended on information from the objects.

Lo indicated her choice by resting her nose on the selected stimulus for more than 3 s and retracting her whiskers. Correct choices produced a whistle followed by fish. The whistle served as a **conditioned reinforcer**, a previously learned signal marking success before the primary food reward arrived.

Stimulus positions changed between trials, so the same command could not be solved by approaching one permanent location. After learning, decisions during exploration took less than 1 s and accuracy approached complete target identification. The command controlled task initiation, while sensory discrimination controlled which object was selected.

slides.title: Whisker adjustments precede head corrections
body: Ball balancing requires continuous adjustments as the supported object changes orientation. Milne and Grant recorded California sea lions named Gina, Anya, and Elmo performing this familiar trained action. The animals received ball-balancing commands and maintained the action until a trainer marked completion.

**Whisker asymmetry** describes the difference between average whisker angles on the two sides of the face. Changes in this measure followed ball orientation more closely and sooner than changes in head orientation. The reported average delays were approximately 27 ms for whiskers and 129 ms for the head.

Balancing therefore recruits control of the sensory array as well as movement of the larger support surface. Whisker movements need not merely follow the head passively. The supplied recording preserves the brief analyzed interval at its original speed, in which ball position and whisker configuration change together.

slides.title: Banking turns recruit the hindflippers
body: Sea lions propel ordinary forward swimming with their foreflippers, while the hindflippers can trail behind. A **banking turn** combines rolling the body with changing the swimming direction. Leahy and colleagues trained sea lions to complete 180° turns beneath an underwater viewing window.

At turn onset, the animal abducted its foreflippers, moving them away from the body, and rolled approximately 90°. The hindflippers spread and rotated, expanding their surface area. Their position behind the body’s center of gravity allows a hydrodynamic force to influence body orientation as well as the path of travel.

The hindflippers’ average **angle of attack**, their orientation relative to the approaching flow, was about 28° during turning. They remained spread during the maneuver and were adducted, brought together, as forward swimming resumed. Coordinated control therefore changes the role of an appendage with the behavioral requirement.

slides.title: Leaping alternates propulsion and body stabilization
body: **Porpoising** is a swimming pattern that repeatedly carries the body above and below the water surface. A trained California sea lion performed consecutive leaps while cameras recorded aerial and submerged phases. The full cycle lasted about 1.5 s in the analyzed captive performance.

The foreflippers generated propulsive strokes during submerged swimming. The hindflippers spread beneath the water and helped stabilize the posterior body region. At the fully aerial crest, the flippers were held against the body or folded rather than continuously generating force against water.

Water entry began with the nose along a curved path, followed by repositioning the foreflippers and hindflippers for the submerged phase. Hindflipper angle of attack during the analyzed submerged phase averaged about 15°. The coordinated cycle thus changes the timing and orientation of several body parts as the surrounding medium changes.

slides.title: Wild porpoising retains the coordinated movement pattern
body: Wild California sea lions in Monterey Bay also executed repeated porpoising leaps. The field recordings and the trained-animal recordings supplied different contexts for the same broad locomotor pattern. Both involved alternating aerial movement with submerged propulsion and a changing hindflipper posture.

In the field sequence, the legs generally remained more extended during the aerial phase, and the hindflippers cleared the water. The reported average leap length was 0.81 body lengths and the aerial height was 0.06 body lengths. Expressing distances in body lengths permits comparison across differently sized animals.

The captive sea lion made longer and higher leaps and used a different entry angle. Training conditions can therefore change the scale of a movement without eliminating the coordinated pattern. The original field movie supplies the natural locomotor comparison; these measurements concern body control rather than synchronization to an acoustic pulse.

slides.title: Musical pulse guides movement beyond the training sound
body: A musical recording contains overlapping instruments and events between the regular beats. Ronan coordinated her head movements with Everybody at about 108 bpm and Boogie Wonderland at 130 bpm. Keeping the repeated response organized required selecting a temporal regularity within this more complex acoustic material.

The songs had different exposure histories. Everybody received explicit training after earlier unsuccessful exposure. Boogie Wonderland had been heard briefly before the later transfer test, without that exposure producing entrained bobbing. Prior exposure and reinforced successful performance are distinct learning events.

After training at the native tempo of Boogie Wonderland, Ronan also followed altered versions spanning 104–143 bpm. The same musical material guided different movement rates. Flexibility across these versions links the trained action to the current pulse instead of one fixed speed learned from a familiar recording.

slides.title: A dancing reputation rests on controlled experiments
body: The public description of Ronan as a dancing sea lion refers to a trained head-bob response measured against sound timing. Her scientific contribution was not simply that she moved while music played, but that her movement adapted across rates and persisted through controlled tests.

Novel tempos, musical recordings, silent omissions, and extended trials each challenged a different simple explanation of the behavior. Together they connected the repeating motor response to temporal regularities that varied independently of the original two training examples.

Ronan’s study site was Long Marine Laboratory at UC Santa Cruz. The original researchers’ recordings are the relevant evidence for her timing performance; a publicity recording supplies behavioral context, while quantified trial measurements establish the accuracy, consistency, and transfer of that coordination.

slides.title: Perturbations separate phase from period correction
body: A **phase perturbation** shifts where the sound sequence falls in time while preserving its eventual repetition rate. A **tempo perturbation** changes the interval between successive sounds. These manipulations challenge different components of an already coordinated movement.

**Period** is the duration of one complete cycle. A repeating motor process can correct timing position quickly while changing its preferred period more slowly. Comparing phase and tempo perturbations therefore tested a coupled-oscillator hypothesis: the sound sequence influences a repeating movement process, or **oscillator**. Transient behavior measures how ongoing coordination changes after an unexpected timing disturbance.

body: The stimulus clicks combined tones at 659 and 1319 Hz for 10 ms. Repeating these brief events created a clear temporal sequence. The main baseline rate was 85 bpm, a rate Ronan had not previously encountered in training or testing.

slides.title: The first transfer response already tracks the change
body: The first presentation of each perturbation provided a test before repeated experience with that exact change. Ronan retained organized movement relative to the beat after these first encounters, including phase changes and persistent changes in the stimulus interval.

body: The researchers aligned trials at the perturbation and compared the relative phase of successive head bobs. Before the change, movement and sound were already coordinated. The sudden phase disturbance created a measurable error that could then be followed over later cycles.

body: Following a lasting rate change, Ronan’s initial movement period and the new stimulus period differed. Head movements therefore had to adjust across several cycles to approach a stable relationship with the new continuing sound sequence.

slides.title: A double bob exposes an immediate motor adjustment
body: During some large slowing perturbations, the next sound occurred when Ronan’s head was near the high point of a movement rather than its low point. She sometimes made an additional small nod before slowing the broader movement cycle.

slides.title: Timing concentration and timing offset are separate
body: A series of movements can be consistently early, consistently late, or widely scattered around the beat. The average phase describes the center of that relationship, whereas the concentration of phases describes how consistently successive movements occupy that position.

Ronan’s post-perturbation phases were tightly concentrated across the tested conditions. Some conditions nevertheless retained systematic offsets. High consistency therefore describes reliable coordination with the sequence and does not automatically mean that the chosen movement landmark coincides exactly with sound onset.

The researchers evaluated these properties separately because different aspects of the timing process influence them. Correcting a disturbance may stabilize a relationship before eliminating its offset, and a repeating behavioral process can remain strongly coordinated while occupying a stable position ahead of or behind the sound.

slides.title: Sign order controls object-directed actions
body: Rocky, a California sea lion, learned hand signs that specified objects, their attributes, and actions. A standard instruction could designate a destination, pause, identify an object by modifiers, and request transport. **Conditional discrimination** means that the appropriate response depends on the preceding cues as well as the currently available objects.

Gisiner and Schusterman recorded orienting during each sign and the final action after a release cue. During 70 anomalous-order probes, 62 orienting responses followed the previously learned sequential rules. The final responses included 55 refusals to complete the command and 15 partial actions.

A modifier narrowed which object Rocky should select, whereas an action sign specified what to do with it. Reordering familiar signs changed the behavior despite retaining familiar components. The experiment connected learned cue order with visual search, waiting at the station, and object-directed movement.

slides.title: Identity matching transfers to unfamiliar shapes
body: **Matching-to-sample** is a choice task in which an initial sample determines the correct comparison. In identity matching, the correct comparison has the same appearance as the sample. Rocky and Rio viewed a sample for approximately 4 s before the two comparison windows opened; a release cue followed after another 2–4 s.

Kastak and Schusterman trained 15 two-stimulus problems and then tested 15 novel problems. Training required 90% correct choices over two consecutive sessions. Correct comparison positions were balanced between left and right, preventing a fixed side response from solving the task.

One sea lion met all transfer criteria on the second test and the other on the third. Both subsequently applied identity matching to stimuli learned previously under different arbitrary matching relations. The learned relationship between sample and choice could therefore guide action when the particular stimulus combination changed.

slides.title: Shared outcomes organize learned stimulus classes
body: A **functional stimulus class** contains different stimuli that acquire a shared behavioral role. Reichmuth Kastak and colleagues presented two sea lions with 20 visual patterns divided into two sets of 10. In simple discrimination sessions, one set produced correct choices and the other produced incorrect choices; reversing the assignment changed which set was rewarded.

Sessions contained 40 trials in four blocks of 10, with stimulus positions balanced between left and right. The animals acquired classes through repeated reversals, then transferred the class relationships to matching-to-sample. In that task, the sample determined which comparison belonged to the appropriate learned class.

Correct responses to the different classes produced class-specific fish reinforcers. Subsequent experiments related new patterns to established classes through these outcomes. Learning linked visual cues and expected consequences, allowing a nose-touch choice to depend on prior reinforcement relationships rather than physical resemblance alone.

slides.title: Hama matches human actions beyond specific commands
body: Hama, a Steller sea lion, had already learned a repertoire of actions through hand signals and verbal commands. Sasaki and colleagues trained a **do-as-I-do** response, in which a human action becomes the model for the animal’s action. Demonstrating “stand,” a head movement, or a tongue action replaced the usual specific cue.

The human initially paired demonstrations with familiar cues, then reduced those prompts. Hama subsequently matched most tested body actions with both a familiar trainer and an unfamiliar demonstrator. Several actions were familiar to her but had not been taught through the demonstration procedure.

Transfer separated general action matching from simply repeating the three demonstrations used during initial training. Performance also depended on what kind of action was attempted: novel body-oriented responses were easier than novel object manipulations. The acquired relationship linked observed body movement with selection from Hama’s own action repertoire.

slides.title: A Go cue separates remembering from immediate copying
body: In a second procedure, Hama watched a complete human demonstration while remaining still, then acted upon the verbal cue “Go.” **Response inhibition** is withholding an action that would otherwise occur. The final cue therefore specified when to respond, while the preceding demonstration specified what to do. Blocking the demonstrator during the response removed ongoing visual guidance as a requirement. slides.title: Precise timing can include an anticipatory offset
body: A **negative asynchrony** occurs when the selected movement landmark precedes the sound. In Ronan’s 2025 snare tests, the average phase at 112 and 120 bpm was negative, while the average at 128 bpm was slightly positive.

This timing pattern is inconsistent with treating every head bob as a delayed reaction initiated only after each sound occurs. A repeating movement can be scheduled in anticipation of the next event while continuing to receive timing information from the current acoustic sequence.

At the same time, anticipation need not place every movement exactly at zero phase. Coordination can be stable and predictive with a systematic offset. Describing the signed relationship preserves that biological timing pattern instead of reducing the response to a simple success-versus-failure label.

body: The human comparison separately evaluated performed tempo, variability of movement intervals, and timing relative to sound onset. These dimensions answer different behavioral questions: how fast the repeated action runs, how consistently it repeats, and where it falls within the external cycle.

slides.title: Human gross movements vary across individuals
body: Humans in the comparison were non-musicians performing a large arm movement rather than a familiar tapping task. Their synchronization differed among individuals, with some participants producing less consistent movement intervals and more variable phases than others.

The distribution of performance matters because a comparison with only a hypothetical perfectly regular human would conceal the range of actual behavior. The experiment measured the same sound sequences in both species and retained each participant’s timing profile.

The study found no consistent rapid improvement across the brief human testing sequence. Ronan, in contrast, entered with a long history of the head-bob task. The observed comparison therefore describes an experienced sea lion and humans performing the specified large-amplitude coordination task, with their different task histories made explicit.

slides.title: Long-term performance includes improved phase alignment
body: At the familiar simple-stimulus rates, Ronan’s later phase alignment was much closer to zero than in several early conditions. The large negative offsets recorded at slower rates in 2013 were substantially reduced when those stimuli were retested after longitudinal experience.

Improvement involved more than bringing the average movement rate near the stimulus. The timing landmark moved closer to the sound onset, and successive movements became more consistent. Rate, phase, and consistency therefore changed together in the later performance profile.

The 108 bpm condition already had a phase near zero in the early experiment, leaving less room for improvement on that particular measure. This condition-specific pattern connects the long-term result to the actual starting performance rather than assuming identical improvement at every tested rate.

slides.title: The tested skill is flexible beat synchronization
body: Ronan’s experiments established coordination with regular pulse sequences and with musical recordings that contain a regular pulse. **Beat synchronization** is the alignment of a repeated action with those pulse events, with flexibility across rates and acoustic forms.

More complex musical abilities involve additional structure, such as grouping beats into recurring patterns or coordinating with deliberately irregular sequences. The 2025 paper distinguished the measured beat-keeping skill from these broader questions about musical organization.

That distinction changes the scientific interpretation: flexible auditory–motor timing is experimentally supported in this sea lion, while complete human-like musical competence was not the tested outcome. The behavioral result still provides a substantial comparative example of prediction, repeated movement, transfer, and adjustment to external rhythm.

slides.title: Rats move near musical beats without task training
body: Ito and colleagues attached a lightweight wireless accelerometer to rats and measured small head movements while music played. An **accelerometer** measures acceleration along specified axes, allowing movement changes to be quantified without requiring a trained beat-marking action.

The rats listened to Mozart’s Sonata for Two Pianos, K.448, at its original rate and at altered playback speeds. Their movements were more strongly aligned with the musical beats near the original tempo, approximately 132 bpm, than at the very fast versions.

This preparation differed from Ronan’s explicitly trained head-bob task. It measured spontaneous small movements during listening rather than an operantly reinforced criterion response. The contrast provides two experimental routes to auditory–motor relationships: acquiring a reliable instructed action and measuring naturally occurring timing during sound exposure.

slides.title: Jerk detects rapid changes in head movement
body: **Jerk** is the rate of change of acceleration. The rat study used this quantity to identify brief movement changes during musical listening. A small movement with a rapid change in acceleration can therefore contribute strongly to the measured response.

Researchers compared jerk near putative beats with jerk elsewhere in the beat cycle. This beat contrast quantified whether the movement signal was organized around the musical pulse instead of being uniformly distributed through time.

At the original musical tempo, the rats showed beat-related movement contrast. Faster playback weakened that organization. The measured response therefore depended on the sound’s temporal scale, connecting the music rate to the timing of small spontaneous movements rather than only to the overall amount of activity.

slides.title: Rat and human movements favor similar tempos
body: The experiment also measured head movements in humans listening to the same musical excerpt at altered speeds. This provided a comparison in which both species were exposed to the same changing temporal structure, although their absolute movement magnitudes differed.

Beat-related movement organization was strongest near the original musical rate rather than at the greatly accelerated versions. The two species also showed related changes in movement strength across individual beats of the original excerpt.

Inspection of the stimulus and motion timing indicated that many movements occurred predictively near the upcoming beat. In this preparation, beat-related organization emerged during listening without Ronan’s explicit synchronization training, broadening the experimental evidence beyond a single kind of instructed motor task.

slides.title: Population activity is tuned to musical event timing
body: The rat study separately recorded **multiunit activity**, the combined spiking response of several nearby neurons, while presenting music at different playback speeds. Activity following beat events was compared with activity following other events in the same musical sequence.

Neural beat contrast was greatest around the original tempo and weakened at much faster speeds. The response also differed among positions in the repeating beat pattern, connecting neural activity to the temporal organization of the musical excerpt rather than merely its presence.

These recordings and the movement measurements were separate experimental assays. Their shared tempo preference linked a candidate neural timing process with the behavioral preference, while the authors used further click stimuli and a model to examine how adaptation could generate that pattern of sensitivity.

slides.title: Short-term adaptation favors intermediate rhythms
body: **Short-term adaptation** is a change in responsiveness during recent stimulation. Repeated sounds can reduce a neural population’s response, with recovery depending on the time since preceding stimulation. This creates a temporal dependence even when each sound is acoustically similar.

Ito and colleagues tested click sequences with three clicks and a rest at 60, 120, 240, and 480 bpm. Recorded responses distinguished beat positions most strongly near an intermediate rate. Very slow sequences and very rapid sequences produced different balances of adaptation and recovery.

The authors’ adaptation model reproduced the intermediate-rate preference and related it to the timing structure of musical material. This is a hypothesis about a candidate neural computation; the sea-lion experiments independently established flexible movement correction, rather than directly measuring that rat adaptation process in Ronan.
